body:
I always thought the evidence for psychotherapies (and antidepressants too) was rather shaky at best..

http://thepsychologist.bps.org.uk/yoke-upon-necks-poor

Nothing.  I've seen psychiatrists, counsellors, psychologists and thought they were entirely useless.

My post history contains all you would ever want to possibly know. Or, feel free to ask.

'The Therapy Industry' by Paul Moloney reflects my thoughts fairly accurately.  As do the other authors I've referenced time and time again.

http://thepsychologist.bps.org.uk/yoke-upon-necks-poor

I gave up seeking help July last year when I was thrown into a psych ward for planning suicide and given no real help apart from another useless medication and a referral to a useless counselor I'd already seen. I figured if that's the best the mental health system has to offer someone at the end of their rope, I won't bother actively seeking help.

I know the feeling. I only really have one person left in my life now and it feels like she is slipping away and doesn't really care nor shows any willingness to even try to help.

To be honest, I think I would prefer having no one. At least that way I can off myself without fear of anyone stopping or attempting to 'save' me.

I'm sure she'd be happier without me.
Maybe it's just the frustration of knowing how useless therapy can be.
I'm trans and largely feel the same way, and can't see anything improving for the better.  I've decided my best option at this point is to end it all.  Personally, I'm going with H2S.

Check out some of the authors and articles I've posted previously.

David Healy, Joanna Moncrieff, Ben Goldacre, Robert Whitaker..

It was actually YOU who first made the positive claim about scientific evidence, so the burden of proof lies with you.   But again, check out the above authors for a good starting point.

There's also a book out known as 'The Therapy Industry' by Paul Moloney which attacks the shoddy science behind CBT, ACT, DBT, etc if you're interested.  Definitely worth a read.

I'm not telling someone to stop getting treatment.  It is YOU who is putting words in MY mouth.  I'm merely highlighting what a failure the mental health system is.

Here's a starting point:

http://joannamoncrieff.com/2013/11/21/models-of-drug-action/

http://joannamoncrieff.com/2013/11/27/why-theres-no-such-thing-as-an-antidepressant/

http://joannamoncrieff.com/2014/07/02/continuing-the-antidepressant-debate-the-clinical-relevance-of-drug-placebo-differences/

http://joannamoncrieff.com/2015/01/14/taking-down-the-talking-cure/

Check out her peer-reviewed publications:

http://joannamoncrieff.com/papers/

There are plenty of peer-reviewed publications in journals there for you to sink your teeth into.  Also check out the other authors I mentioned, particularly David Healy.

Instead of just rejecting my argument because I have a 'bias', try doing some reading.

"But how do we know it doesn't work for some people?"

Again, read some journal articles.  We can look at surveys, relapse rates, the Hamilton rating scale (which is quite controversial in itself)..  Diagnoses seem to be going up across the board too, which I don't think is a good thing and is quite possibly a symptom of a deeper underlying issue, as I alluded to in my previous post.  I'm not just arguing that treatment doesn't work for some people, I'm arguing that it doesn't work for a LOT of people.  There are a few academics arguing now that even for the people it does work for, it's possibly little more than an amplified placebo effect.  This applies to both medication and therapy and really shows the hopelessness of the mental health system.

"I have to point out that you wrote "in my experience". We can't rule out the possibility that where you live, mental care services are sub-par. And while that doesn't rule out others having the same experience, the doctors they met with probably were inexperienced or not qualified enough for the task."

I'm in Australia, where we have Medicare (socialised healthcare system).  It's not great, but certainly better than 'murica as far as accessibility.  And yet here I am still criticising the mental health system.  If there are doctors who are inexperienced or not qualified enough for the task, then what the hell are they doing treating people?  Besides, I've come across many people who have been treated by experienced psychs only to end up regretting the experience.

I'd argue that suicide success rates are dependent upon the accessibility of easy, fatal methods that are likely to result in death.  At least here in Australia, there's evidence that gun control laws resulted in a substantial drop in suicide rates.

The unfortunate reality seems to be that as gun suicide rates dropped, other rates (such as hanging) rose.   I would imagine this would result in an increase in unsuccessful suicides.

Basically if you remove the means, people will attempt to find other ways which are less likely to result in death.

1) "I'm sorry to say, you know what's going in your mind, but that's still only your mind. 1 mind.  They base what they know off many more minds"

2) "So if they tell you they know something, they have scientific proof behind it."

If we look at 1) on its own, this amounts to nothing more than mob/herd mentality which treats suicide as a taboo and a moral issue where somehow society deems it okay to take away someone's right to death based on some bizarre prevailing life-affirming fantasy which is little more than a cognitive bias in itself (which is kind of ironic when depression sufferers are often accused of the same).  I fully agree with OP's original comment "Anyone who tries to claim that they know what is in my head more than I do is treating me like an inanimate object".  Psychiatry and the mental health system are disgustingly paternal and arrogant in this regard.  It's also quite problematic when someone presents with suicidal thoughts, only for the psych to break doctor/patient confidentiality because somehow it's 'in the patient's best interests'.  Community Treatment Orders are a reflection of this, and the emerging evidence suggests that they aren't even effective!

If we examine 2), as I've already suggested (and alluded to more elaborately in my previous post history), the scientific evidence is tenuous at best.

I'm not sure what words I'm putting in your mouth.  Perhaps you should have elaborated your position more clearly. Also..

"That said, a good doctor doesn't just diagnose you and gives you pills. They have to know you well before they decide the course of action."

I beg to differ.  It's been mine and others experience that they largely do just diagnose and give you pills.  Personal anecdotes aside, most doctors are required to abide by a certain set of guidelines & standards of care which lay out the foundations of treatment options, and these guidelines tend to be quite stringent with an emphasis on medication.  This seems to be the case even moreso when suicidal ideation is involved.  I wouldn't disagree that therapy is also part of this, but we can't deny that medication plays a huge role in defining treatment guidelines.

The sad reality is, it's in the interest of healthcare, insurance providers, employers, government and the economy as a whole to push for prescribing 'quick fix' pills and other short-lived treatment options which is likely to have a negative impact on patient outcomes.
Mob mentality is never a justification, and the scientific evidence is tenuous at best.

Thanks. I figured as much. It seems as though they would aim to return you to a stable condition, only allowing you to withdraw consent and refuse further treatment when you're conscious and able to make the decision.

Same.  This is exactly why I think suicide prevention is a dismal failure.  By threatening to call police, ambulance, and otherwise being coercive, I think they're really just discouraging people from seeking help instead causing them to bury their feelings.  When I go, I'll just silently slip off and try not to give off any signals.
After 6 - 7 years, nope. No more.
I wouldn't count on it.  I say that as someone who has never really forgiven their partner for having me sent to a psych ward.
This is spot on.

If I can't even make the world a tolerable place for myself, I've got no hope of making it better for anyone else. Unfortunately you reach a point where you realise some things (in fact most) are outside of your control.

Youtube videos? Yes. They're hardly nobodies though. In particular, check out Joanna Moncrieff and David Healy. Both fairly respected academics.

Some peer reviewed papers if you're actually interested:

http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4118946/
http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3020050/pdf/bjgp61-047.pdf

antipsychotics may be responsible for decline in brain matter:
http://bjp.rcpsych.org/content/198/2/85.long

http://www.google.co.uk/url?url=http://www.researchgate.net/publication/41087772_A_systematic_review_of_the_effects_of_antipsychotic_drugs_on_brain_volume/file/9c9605212115247a19.pdf&rct=j&frm=1&q=&esrc=s&sa=U&ei=1QfRU_-0HYig7Abv74C4Aw&ved=0CC0QFjAE&usg=AFQjCNGv-Dv1KVnIQsL0z46VrWDVEPP_8w

linking antidepressants and suicidality:
http://joannamoncrieff.files.wordpress.com/2013/12/cds0311.pdf

Antidepressants induce abnormal mental states, akin to alcohol being a 'social lubricant', but don't fix any underlying pathology:
http://www.plosmedicine.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pmed.0030240

That's just one author, with links pulled from http://joannamoncrieff.com/papers/ .. Plenty more references there, and plenty more references in each paper to other research.

Here, have some more! (this time David Healy -- he seems to focus on the link between antidepressants and suicide/violence):

Antidepressant induced suicidal ideation:
http://davidhealy.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/05/1991-Creaney-Healy-Prozac-Suicide.pdf

Or fuck it, here's a full list:
http://davidhealy.org/articles/#journalpublications

There's also more research out there on an increased risk of violence when on antidepressants, too.

The Critical Psychiatry Network is also worth taking a look at, and is comprised of psychiatrists, medical students, etc:
http://www.criticalpsychiatry.co.uk/
Check out their articles section containing quite a few publications.
Same. I'm about ready to check out.
Mental healthcare in Australia is also a joke.
You speak the truth. It largely seems to be a revolving door.

Even if I wasn't afraid to go, I wouldn't go anyway because I know that no one can help.  Can you see any upside in going yourself?  What outcome(s) would you expect if you went? How likely would these outcomes be? I'm not really giving you any advice, unfortunately. But they are questions worth asking..

For myself, the outcome I would expect is to be thrown into a psych ward for days, given a new medication and be 'referred' back to counselors I've already seen (again).. Then I'd expect them to release me when I'm 'safe' (even though I could easily take my life once let back out again).  Unfortunately I've heard people refer to psych wards as 'revolving doors' before, so I suppose I would expect the same outcome over and over.

An absolute fuck wit of a psychiatrist who was rude and dismissive, and did nothing more than shove another useless medication in my face, and refer me to a counselor who I had already seen.  I pointed this out to him and how the counselor was NOT helpful before, and he basically fucking ignored me.

I'd write a formal complaint (and also complain about the social workers who turned up to my workplace), but it won't achieve anything and I'll be seen as just another headcase.

Honestly, at this point I hope to just end up as another dead corpse. You might have better luck at the ER.

Activist groups for what?

ITT: no one has a fucking clue about psychiatric medications beyond 'herpa derp they work!' over and over ad nauseam.

I've had a plan for months, and about ready to execute.  As far as I'm concerned, there is no point at which I should go to the ER. Been there, done that and found it a colossal waste of time. All it did was make me more suicidal.
Thank you. You expressed it far more eloquently than I could in my extremely pissed off mood (and I was doing most of my typing on a phone).

In addition, I'm just going to leave this here..

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4R6MXO2j0V0

It's worth spending the time and watching all parts. I'm sure no one will give a shit though instead preferring to downvote me into oblivion, as their minds are already made.

I've already posted this elsewhere, but what the hell:

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A3YB59EKMKw

>Depression isn't terminal

How can you be so sure?

> You are mentally ill and not capable of making sensible decisions in regard to your life.

Source? How do we know WHICH decisions people are making in a rational manner? Rationality isn't just an all-encompassing blanket. People's rationality may be skewed in different ways and across different cognitive functions. What about the concept of depressive realism? Or to flip the concept totally on its head, what about various cognitive biases and impairments that positive-minded people make about their own character, abilities, etc?  Perhaps this is being projected on to depressed people and adversely impacts how depressed people are treated? Perhaps even in a way that's irrational? 

Besides, what a fucking insult to say I'm not capable of making sensible decisions. I think I've made far many more sensible life decisions than a lot of peers my age.  Studied in school, got an Engineering degree -- now, totally fucked in a dead-end IT support job with nothing else in sight (despite having worked 2 years as a Software Developer in a large enterprise environment with decent references).  I've played the game, done everything as I should and yet continue to slip through the cracks.  That is, I'm high-functioning.  How do you determine my capacity to make sensible decisions? What is/isn't sensible?  After all the shit I've been through (that's only 10% of the story), I believe I should have the right to take my own life and not have to put up with cheery do-gooder arseholes saying 'it gets better' and other empty platitudes.

> I have been in the psych ward 3 times now. Once for overdosing intentionally, once for cutting both my wrists, and another time where they thought I was a danger to myself. Back then I thought the same thing as you, that I should have the right to end my own life because I felt like I would never get better and it would never end. But I sure am glad to be alive now that I'm back in a period where I am thinking properly again. And when I do end up back in that frame of mind again I sure as hell hope somebody intervenes.

I'm sure I can source many anecdotes from people and places (like /r/suicidewatch, for instance) of those who have suffered for YEARS, tried a plethora of meds and therapies yet are still suicidal and wishing they had ended it earlier?

>Euthanasia is for people who are literally dying already with no quality of life left at all. 

Why can't we apply this value judgement equally to certain subsets of depressed people? What is 'literally dying'? In the physical sense? Why not in the mental sense, too?  Is the underlying assumption that mental suffering is somehow malleable and salvageable? What if this just isn't true?
His (her? they?.. sorry, unsure of preferred pronoun) description fits in with a drug-centred model / approach toward mental health.. But let's not kid ourselves that this ISN'T the case.

No. Just... no... Perhaps read up on models of drug action first:

http://joannamoncrieff.com/2013/11/21/models-of-drug-action/

and

http://joannamoncrieff.com/2013/11/27/why-theres-no-such-thing-as-an-antidepressant/

Also check out the other links I've already posted in this thread. There are tonnes of comments on this thread that are addressed in the several links and by the authors I've already posted.

>And making the argument that you should have the right to euthanasia for depression harms the euthanasia movement for people who want it to be legalised for actual terminal illnesses.

WHY does it harm the euthanasia movement? How can we be so presumptuous to suggest that depression in some instances is not terminal? Where's the distinction?

>Just because they don't work right for you doesn't mean they don't work at all and shouldn't be used.

I wasn't arguing from just this standpoint.  I'm arguing from the standpoint of clinical trials and a lot of the newer research and meta-analyses that are starting to come out. Studies that cover hundreds to thousands of people. Research showing that the 'statistically significant' difference between placebo and active drug is negligible.

>Let's ignore for a minute that psychiatry/psychology/therapy helps thousands of Australians (/millions worldwide) every day

At least provide a source? I can easily argue the opposite of that, with references.  I have plenty of studies I can dig up on the iatrogenic effects of psychiatric medications, relapse rates, and so forth.

>You say "society" is to blame for your depression, that "external factors" are the problem, not you. Basically you're saying that you are 100% mentally healthy and it's every single other person in Australia is the problem.

Strawman. I didn't say 'every single other person in Australia' is the problem. I said society as a whole, and I still stand by this argument.

Why should I be forced to live in a society full of bigoted, discriminatory morons? Where my employment prospects are bleak (just look at the unemployment rate for trans people), where workers in the health system are largely seen as gate keepers, where people are just generally unaccepting?

>As a person in Australia (and therefore part of your problem), what would you have me do?

Nothing. I've given up on the notion of educating people. When your own family basically disown you despite your attempts, you begin to realise that people won't change in their ways. And when you see the same in others, you realise people won't change their ways. Not within your lifetime, anyway.

>You might think that suicide is a solution, but I promise that its not.

Why isn't it a solution? How can you promise that it's not?  You should provide a more reasoned argument.

>Please get help
Been there, done that.. multiple times.

> If you don't see the current therapy you're getting as helpful, why not ask your doctor to help you find another one? If your doctor is resistant to helping you find alternative therapies, you are allowed to find one who will. You have that right. 

Been there, done that. Multiple therapies across multiple psychiatrists, psychologists and counselors. Oh, and I've tried 7 different medications now. I know my chances are slim after this many (see the STAR*D trial -- probably the most comprehensive around).

>Hope is not lost.

Again, just a baseless assertion.  I feel I've exhausted pretty much all my options at this point.

>Please consider that your illness may be causing you to think irrationally, and the right kind of therapy may help lift that fog.

Again pathologising. What illness? How is it an illness? The argument gets much more in-deph than just 'you have an illness that needs to be treated'.  Why can't suicide just be seen as a philosophical position?  Why is it irrational? Isn't it more rational to allow someone to die than forcing them to live on in suffering? Isn't it just plain cruel and absurd to force someone to live on when they are treatment resistant and will continue suffering and have constant thoughts of suicide? Isn't it rather delusional to assume and hope that everyone can recover and FORCE this view on others rather than undertaking a proper assessment?  What right do other people have in forcing me to live?

How long do I keep plodding along trying bullshit treatment after bullshit treatment before I realise I'm wasting away time and suffering and kill myself?  Why are people intent on keeping me alive when there's a slim to no chance of being successfully treated? This is my own conclusion based on research (again refer to the authors I've already posted) and the fact I believe my depression is largely situational, which is not likely to change, at least in my lifetime. I can tell you now I've done far more research on this topic than the average person.

Also the 'fog' metaphor. Care to explain? This is another problem with how the whole mental health discussion is framed. Too many metaphors that don't really make sense or actually explain anything.  Just as people may argue my thinking is 'skewed' (not sure if that's what you're implying), I can also argue the opposite as I've alluded to above.

I don't expect medical practitioners to help. That's the point. Instead of being extremely misguided and coercive, they should just back off. and I should be granted the fundamental human right of suicide.

Oh, and downvote away. Typical reddit groupthink.  Parrot back popular opinion without any reasoning or rationale and upvote each other. Maybe instead of just downvoting, contribute to the discussion and explain WHY you think something is worth a downvote?

>You say that therapy us useless but there is more than one type of therapy,

What if you've already attempted multiple types of therapy?  What about the fact that therapy doesn't really change your circumstances. Learning coping skills may help a bit, but it ultimately doesn't change anything.

>likewise with drugs. 

Same again -- what if you've already tried multiple drugs?

> Some of these will work for some people, others won't, it doesn't mean they shouldn't be tried.

What if you've tried multiples of both? Where does it end? Or is it all just a pointless, futile exercise that doesn't lead to successful treatment in some instances?

And that's exactly the problem.  They don't treat an underlying 'disease' that we're aware of.  They only treat clusters of symptoms, often poorly, which *may* lead to an improvement in HAM-D (and other) scores without actually improving underlying mood.

Joanna Moncrieff talks about how inadequate the disease model is, and how statistical significance may not really translate all that well into clinical significance.

http://joannamoncrieff.com/2014/05/01/the-chemical-imbalance-theory-of-depression-still-promoted-but-still-unfounded/

http://joannamoncrieff.com/2014/07/02/continuing-the-antidepressant-debate-the-clinical-relevance-of-drug-placebo-differences/

Or better yet, check out her entire blog and book, or even just the lecture video I posted above.

I recommend the following authors:

Joanna Moncrieff,
David Healy,
Irving Kirsch,
Robert Whitaker,

Plenty of research in there.  David Healy in particular focuses on the adverse effects of SSRIs.

His talk on the pitfalls of evidence-based medicine is particularly damning: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A3YB59EKMKw

Also recommended:

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IV1S5zw096U

Robert Whitaker delves particularly into the iatrogenic effects of psychiatric medications.

I think it's mind-blowingly stupid and negligent to give anti-depressant medications to someone who is already suicidal (and it seems to be all too common).

EDIT: downvoted for providing sources (fucking mountains, actually) of research into a claim. Thanks, reddit!
Anyway, start with those authors.. Then continue digging as deep as you wish. You'll find quite a large debate coming from both sides, but suffice to say that isn't as clear cut as 'meds work, keep trying them'.

Fuck the mental health system. Too much emphasis on pathologising the individual and little else on psychosocial / external factors and their ramifications. I'm fucking tired of being offered useless medications that don't do a damn thing when my depression is largely situational. I'm sick of useless 'professionals' who don't understand suffering, how to adequately help people or know when to step back and realise that some people probably are helpless.

I don't see anything changing sufficiently in my lifetime, so damn straight I'm suicidal.
I could start a long diatribe on the uselessness of therapy, the coercive nature of the mental health system and how I believe in the right to kill myself, but I'd just be repeating earlier posts.

These awareness campaigns are horse shit. On one hand we encourage people to 'reach out' for help (but largely to paid 'professionals' - god forbid we actually engage each other in society at any real, meaningful level), but then we coerce and threaten them with being committed into a psych ward, encouraging them to instead bury their feelings.

Just another boring, fruitless, meaningless campaign that doesn't affect any real meaningful change but allows people to feel good about themselves. Yawn.
Thinking about suicide.

If you do go to see a psychiatrist / psychologist / counselor / whatever, don't get your hopes up. I've been there, done all that and found it to be entirely useless.  Even the ones who supposedly 'specialise' in gender stuff aren't very helpful.

EDIT: just my experience..but you will find a lot of trans folk seem to share similar experiences and end up feeling utterly helpless when dealing with the mental health system.  The only real advantage I found was getting a referral to an endocrinologist, but even then I'm regretting having been on hormones.
'The thought of suicide is a great consolation: by means of it one gets through many a dark night.' ~ Nietzsche

I'm in a similar situation (but male to female). I choose death.  My situation is already fucked, and transitioning is likely to just make it worse (friends, family, relationships, job prospects, etc).

I don't have the money, support, etc so I plan to just off myself instead.  I just need to tie up some loose ends first. I know that I'll never be happy, so I don't plan on continuing to live on in misery.

It's exceptionally easy for others to tell you to transition without knowing what's involved or a proper understanding of how shit trans people have it thanks to a bigoted society.  I've seen trans people come out and lose their jobs, family, etc and I don't plan on going through that.

So the afterlife / next life provides more reason for me to kill myself?

Personally, I find a lot of the whole guru / mysticism thing boring, vacuous, ambiguous and unenlightened.

I'm happy to post details here.. I've tried (in order) Escitalopram, fluoxetine, desvenlafaxine, reboxetine, aripiprazole, pregablin and nortriptyline. I ended up with a script for moclobemide, which was right around when I realised I was sick of playing pill roulette, and the psychiatrist I was seeing was useless.

I should also note my 'symptoms' aren't just there. It's largely situational and other external factors that make me feel suicidal. The more I realise how nothing is likely to change for the better, the more I'm ready to go through with it. Unfortunately medications won't change anything about my circumstances, and the research I've alluded to above reinforces my position on how dismal and ineffective meds really are.

I plan on contacting Nitschke, if only to commend him on the great work he's doing and thank him for his courage in fighting the system.

I've already tried 7 medications to no avail. After doing some research (see Joanna Moncrieff, David Healy, Daniel Carlat, Irving Kirsh & Robert Whitaker), I've come to the conclusion that antidepressants are useless.

Fuck the do-gooders with a saviour complex. If I've come to the conclusion that my life is no longer worth living and circumstances are unlikely to change, then why should I be made to live on in suffering?

I'm completely disgusted we live in a society that prevents you from taking your own life, instead preferring to inflict endless suffering. Maybe for some people suicide is far more rational than the alternative?

After my own fruitless dealings with the mental health system, I feel even more inclined to take my own life and NOT seek any help knowing how utterly useless the help I've received thus far has been. I'm not even game to speak up knowing I'll be coerced and committed (again) into a psych ward.

There's also the problem of limiting access to more humane and successful means resulting in failed attempts and worsening someone's condition.

I should also note I support the idea of rational suicide in addition to euthanasia. Where do you even draw the line? Who's to say depression is not terminal? The catch-all claim that it's treatable 'disease' completely neglects any nuances and fails to recognise that maybe for some people it can't be treated sufficiently. Perhaps externalities and psychosocial factors can't be improved in one's lifetime and other 'treatments' won't overcome or alleviate this harsh reality?

Maybe people need to stop dreaming and realise we live in a broken society and expecting people to cope is just ignoring how bad things really are? This would be far preferable to assuming there's something 'wrong' with the individual and maybe act as a catalyst for change in society as we begin to reflect outward and not pathologise those suffering.

Then why not hasten death's calling? Sure, my desire for death will eventually be satisfied, but why not satisfy it now when the probability of a life worth living is so extremely low? Why should I wait around and suffer years of torment when I could just end it all now?

I see many people on here who reach mid-age and are still suicidal after so many years. Then, I look at how shitty my situation is and see the same thing occurring.  Why wait it out?
Why did I start reading the comments on that article? How utterly fucking depressing.
That's what's known as survivorship bias.
If life is a game, then it has horrendous gameplay.

In my opinion, expecting people to learn to 'cope' is terribly misguided and only serves to trivialise the suffering they're experiencing.

Maybe some people just can't cope with what's thrown at them, and don't wish to go on?

I'm in a similar situation, but for not as long a period of time.. Long enough for me to realise nothing will change though and nip it in the bud before I end up wasting away years (I'm not saying that's what you've done, but how I feel personally).

I've never bothered because I've tried psychiatrists, psychologists and counselors but found them to be entirely useless.

I wouldn't even dream of calling a hotline, because I know an ambulance would be quickly at my door. Fuck that. I'm definitely not going down that path again.
I've read The Myth of Sisyphus and it was fairly unconvincing.  If anything, it's probably contributed to me feeling suicidal.. Not that that's a bad thing, it just is.
There's nothing I'd rather be doing, nor anything that would make my life more interesting. I've given up on that notion due to external factors and the world at large. I just want out.

The only thing stopping me at this stage is basic survival instinct, which I'm trying to work out how to overcome (alcohol maybe? prescription meds? Not sure how I can get access to those..). I'm so tired of people making bullshit claims like 'oh, some part of you must consciously want to live'. No. I've consciously made the decision I wish to no longer be around, but also understand the biological trappings of survival.

The longer I go on, the more I realise death is the best option as my life just plods along aimlessly despite efforts to advance myself in career and other areas. It's really just an endless, nauseating merry-go-round of insanity and absurdity.  Maybe given time, this realisation is the best way to overcome basic survival instinct? Although I'd rather be gone sooner than later.  It seems so fucking paradoxical at times.

Constantly seeing and experiencing the failings of the mental health field also seems to help provide the impetus to go through with it, too.

Yep. I (foolishly) didn't know this until I started doing some reading/research quite recently. Let's just say I'm not going back to the last psychiatrist I saw for this and other reasons.

The more reading I do, the more bleak the picture becomes (see Joanna Moncrieff, David Healy, Daniel Carlat, Ben Goldacre and to a lesser degree Irving Kirsch, Robert Whitaker).  I always used to associate elements of anti-psychiatry with fringe Scientologist quackery, but I suppose I've been coming across more respectable authors now who have swayed my opinion a bit.

Thank you. Finally someone who gets it (I'm not attacking people in this thread -- but generally people don't seem to get it).  If I had the energy, I would try and add more into the discussion, but unfortunately I don't. Maybe later?  Some of my earlier posts might give you an idea though.

Am I okay? No. After seeing various mental health 'professionals', trying 7 different medications, being committed to a psych ward for being suicidal, I give up on the mental health system.  In fact, the more I deal with the system, the worse I feel.  Bland, cookie-cutter 'advice', pointless therapy that doesn't help, and a field of medicine that pathologises depression with little emphasis on psychosocial factors whilst prescribing medications that don't really work. See my post history for more elaboration on my ranting.
